headline: The US military says it must be ready to fight in space

sources.title: US troops must prepare to fight around the moon, Trump's top military adviser says (Action News Jax / AP)
US Air Force secretary reveals deployment of on-orbit space control weapons (Military Times)
America's troops must prepare now for warfare on moon, top general says (Stars and Stripes)

chunks.text: The US military says it must be ready to fight in space, even near the moon. On September 16, 2026, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff {{spelled out}} that view at a conference in Maryland. The [[joint force]], he said, must fight, [[endure]], and win "from the [[seabed]] to [[cislunar space]]," the region between Earth and the moon. He {{pointed out}} that future wars may not {{play out}} with safe [[rear areas]] or easy access to supplies.

verbs.correct: To explain something clearly and in detail
verbs.wrong: To send a message in secret code
verbs.why: A good contract spells out who pays for repairs. The teacher spelled out the rules on the first day. The chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff spelled out his view on space at a conference in Maryland.

verbs.correct: To tell people about a fact they should notice
verbs.wrong: To refuse to answer a reporter's question
verbs.why: She pointed out a mistake in the report. The guide pointed out that the bridge is 100 years old. The chairman pointed out that future wars may not have safe rear areas.

verbs.correct: To happen and develop in a certain way
verbs.wrong: To stop a plan before it has started
verbs.why: Nobody knows how the election will play out. The trip played out exactly as we hoped. The chairman said future wars may not play out with safe rear areas or easy access to supplies.

chunks.text: Two days earlier, the Air Force secretary {{brought up}} a new fact. He said the Space Force now has weapons in [[orbit]] that can defend US forces against [[hostile]] action. He {{held back}} the details and would not say whether the weapons could physically {{take out}} a target. He said the US has watched China and Russia {{build up}} space [[capabilities]] for more than ten years.

verbs.correct: To mention a subject in a talk
verbs.wrong: To end a meeting before it finishes
verbs.why: He brought up the budget at dinner. The reporter brought up the missing money. Two days before the chairman spoke, the Air Force secretary brought up the weapons in orbit.

verbs.wrong: To send a message to many people
verbs.why: The company held back the test results. Police are holding back some details of the case. The Air Force secretary held back the details of the new space weapons.

verbs.correct: To destroy or disable a target
verbs.why: The storm took out the power lines. A virus took out the office computers. The secretary would not say whether the weapons could physically take out a target.

verbs.correct: To make something bigger or stronger over time
verbs.wrong: To copy another country's plans exactly
verbs.why: The country built up its navy over twenty years. She built up a strong team from nothing. The secretary said the US has watched China and Russia build up space capabilities for more than ten years.

chunks.text: The head of the Space Force's combat command {{laid out}} a [[growth plan]]. The service was {{set up}} in 2019, during Trump's first term. It plans to double its [[personnel]] to about 25,000 within five years. About two-thirds of them will {{carry out}} [[combat]] work. He said humanity is moving deeper into space, and China is active in parts of it. The US must {{keep up}} and be ready for [[operations]] near the moon.

verbs.correct: To present a plan in a clear way
verbs.wrong: To cancel a plan at the last minute
verbs.why: The mayor laid out her plan for the new park. He laid out the schedule for the week. The head of the Space Force's combat command laid out a growth plan.
They set up a charity for sick children. She set up her own company in 2020. The Space Force was set up in 2019, during Trump's first term.

verbs.correct: To do a task or mission
verbs.wrong: To move a plan to a later date
verbs.why: The team carried out the repairs overnight. Doctors carried out the test twice. About two-thirds of the Space Force will carry out combat work.

verbs.correct: To stay at the same level as others
verbs.why: Small shops struggle to keep up with big chains. He runs fast, and I cannot keep up. The Space Force general said the US must keep up as other countries move deeper into space.

chunks.text: China's [[foreign ministry]] {{pushed back}}. Its [[spokesperson]] said China supports the [[peaceful use]] of space and opposes weapons there. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, signed by 95 countries including the US, China, and Russia, {{rules out}} [[nuclear weapons]] in orbit and [[weapons tests]] on the moon. Asked about the [[treaty]], the Space Force general said the service would keep its operations safe and responsible. The news matters now because the US had never described its space weapons so openly.

verbs.correct: To disagree with and resist a claim
verbs.wrong: To repeat a claim many times
verbs.why: The workers pushed back against the new rules. She pushed back when the boss blamed her team. China's foreign ministry pushed back and said it opposes weapons in space.

verbs.correct: To say something is not allowed or possible
verbs.wrong: To sign an agreement with another country
verbs.why: The judge ruled out cameras in the courtroom. The doctor ruled out surgery for now. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty rules out nuclear weapons in orbit.

mainIdea.s: Top US military leaders say the joint force must be ready to fight in space, even near the moon. The Space Force has confirmed weapons in orbit and plans to double in size.
mainIdea.why: The chairman spoke of cislunar space, the Air Force secretary confirmed weapons in orbit, and the Space Force plans to reach about 25,000 people.

mainIdea.s: The Air Force secretary said the US will place weapons in orbit within five years to match China. The Space Force will double its personnel once those weapons are ready.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the weapons are already in orbit. The five-year timeline is for doubling personnel, not for placing weapons.

mainIdea.s: The US and China have signed a new agreement to keep the area around the moon free of all weapons. Both militaries will now share their plans for future lunar missions.
mainIdea.why: No new agreement was signed. The US described weapons already in orbit, and China's foreign ministry objected to weapons in space.

tf.s: The chairman spelled out his view at a conference in Maryland.
tf.why: He spoke there on September 16, 2026, and said the joint force must be ready from the seabed to cislunar space.

tf.s: The Air Force secretary gave full details about the weapons in orbit.
tf.why: He held back the details and would not say whether the weapons could physically take out a target.

tf.s: The Space Force was set up in 2019, during Trump's first term.
tf.why: It was created during Trump's first term and now plans to double its personnel.

tf.s: The Space Force plans to cut its personnel to about 25,000.
tf.why: The growth plan its combat command's head laid out doubles personnel to about 25,000 within five years.

tf.s: China's foreign ministry pushed back against the US statements.
tf.why: Its spokesperson said China supports the peaceful use of space and opposes weapons there.

tf.s: The 1967 treaty rules out weapons tests on the moon.
tf.why: Signed by 95 countries, it also bans nuclear weapons in orbit.
